title: About
text:
This website was created as a project towards the requirements of the Graduate Academic Certificate in Science Communication at McMaster University (2026 - 2027).
I used Claude Sonnet 5.5 to create a template for the Quarto documents, which I then customized for the specific project. The project itself was inspired by Andrew Heiss’ “Visualizing {dplyr}’s mutate(), summarize(), group_by(), and ungroup() with animations” blog post. The interactivity features were inspired by “Parable of the Polygons” created by Vi Hart and Nicky Case.
The data set comes from lterdatasampler, an R package created by the Long Term Ecological Research program (LTER) Network.

title: Visualizing R
text:
To learn about the functions of the tidyverse, we will explore a dataset from the Long Term Ecological Research program Network. This data describes the body size of Fiddler crabs in salt marshes from Florida to Massachusetts during the summer of 2016. You can read more about this data here
Climate change has caused this species to expand its range northward in response to ocean warming. As a result, we can use this data to observe Bergmann’s Rule in action. Bergmann’s Rule predicts that organisms at higher latitudes (more north) will have larger body sizes.
Let’s start exploring the data using R and RStudio to see if the sampled Fiddler crabs follow this prediction.

Exploring the Data
We will need to start by installing the packages needed for these evaluations. We can do that with the install.packages() function. This may take a while, but don’t worry, once you’ve installed the packages on your computer once, you won’t need to do it again.

install.packages(c("lterdatasampler", "ggplot2", "dplyr"))

Now that our packages are installed, we need to load them into our R session. We can do this using the library() function, as shown below. This only needs to be done once per session.

library(lterdatasampler)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

Now that we have the packages loaded, we can get at our data. Let’s call it crab_data.






TipSyntax Alert





The <- symbol assigns a value to a named object in R.
Syntax: name <- value (e.g., x <- 42)
If x doesn’t exist yet, a new object is created; it x does exist, its value is replaced.




crab_data <- data(pie_crab)

Here is the raw data, showing 50 rows of the 392 total. We have columns date in the format YYYY-MM-DD, latitude, site (which is an abbreviated sample location), size (which is carapace size in millimeters), air_temp and air_temp_sd (the air temperature and it’s standard deviation in Celsius), water_temp and water_temp_df (the water temperature and it’s standard deviation), and name (full site name).






TipSyntax Alert





The %>% (or |>) symbol is the forward pipe operator. It takes the value or expression on the left-hand side and passes it as the first argument to the function on the right-hand side.
For example: head(crab_data) is the same as crab_data %>% head()

Plotting Our Data
However, summary statistics only give us a numerical was of seeing the trends. An easy way to quickly see trends in data is to use plotting. Creating plots allows for readers to quickly understand the relationships between variables, without having to compute or sort parameters.
Here we will use the ggplot2 package to visualize the raw data and site means.

Geoms: point and jitter
geom_point() draws one dot per row of your data and places points exactly on their appropriate x and y coordinate, such that if points overlap, you can only see the top one.
geom_jitter() on the other hand, considers the overlapping of points. Using this function instead of geom_point() will place points slightly offset of one another so that individual points are more easily visualized.


Smooth lines
geom_smooth() is a function for ggplots that fits a trend line and confidence band to your data.
There are many available methods that geom_smooth() can use to fit a line to your data, but the most commonly used ones are “lm”, “loess”, and “gam”.
The “lm” option will fit a straight line linear regression to your data.
The “loess” option is the default for geom_smooth(), so if you don’t specify a method it will use “loess” when your dataset has less than 1,000 points. This method fits a curve that follows the local structure of the data.
The “gam” option is best for large data sets (>1,000 observations), which fits a smooth spline.


Themes
But what’s the point of making a plot if you can’t make it pretty! In ggplot2 there are nine built-in themes that control the non-data display elements of your figure. These nine themes are:

theme_grey()
